explain.title: Acids
explain.body: Acids are known for their sour taste and their ability to change blue litmus paper to red. Lemon and curd are examples of everyday substances associated with acids.

explain.title: Natural and mineral acids
explain.body: Acids obtained from natural sources are called natural or organic acids. Mineral or man-made acids are prepared from minerals; hydrochloric acid, sulphuric acid and nitric acid are examples.

explain.title: Bases and alkalis
explain.body: Bases are known for their bitter taste and slippery touch, and they change red litmus paper to blue. An alkali is a base that dissolves in water. Sodium hydroxide and potassium hydroxide are examples.

explain.title: Basic oxides and neutralization
explain.body: Metal oxides can be basic because they react with acids to form salt and water. Sodium oxide also reacts with water to produce sodium hydroxide. When acids and bases cancel each other's properties, the reaction is called neutralization; salt and water form.

mistakes: Do not confuse a base with an alkali: an alkali is specifically a base that dissolves in water.
Do not reverse the litmus changes: acids turn blue litmus red, while bases turn red litmus blue.
Do not confuse the natural source of an organic acid with the acid itself; for example, tamarind is a source of tartaric acid.
When describing neutralization, include both products: a salt and water.
Do not omit state symbols when writing the sodium oxide reaction if they are requested.

modules.title: 7.2 Different Concepts of Acids and Bases

writtenQuestions.text: Q7.5. What is the difference between a strong acid and a concentrated acid?
modelAnswer: A strong acid ionizes to a large extent in water.
A concentrated acid contains a large amount of acid in a given volume of solution.
Therefore, strength depends on ionization, whereas concentration depends on the amount of acid present.
A strong acid is not necessarily concentrated, and a concentrated acid is not necessarily strong.

explain.title: Arrhenius acids
explain.body: An acid is that substance which dissociates in water to give proton (H⁺) or hydronium ion (H₃O⁺). For example, HCl ionizes in water to form H₃O⁺ and Cl⁻.

explain.title: Arrhenius bases
explain.body: A base is that substance which dissociates in water to give hydroxyl ions (OH⁻). For example, NaOH gives Na⁺ and OH⁻ in water.

explain.title: Water and neutralization
explain.body: Water surrounds the ions formed in solution. In a strong acid–strong base neutralization, H₃O⁺ and OH⁻ react to form water and release heat: H₃O⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → 2H₂O(l) + Heat.

explain.title: Strong and weak ionization
explain.body: The strength of an acid depends upon the extent to which it is ionized in water. Mineral acids such as HCl ionize extensively, while organic acids such as acetic acid ionize to a very limited extent. NaOH and KOH are strong bases; NH₄OH is a weak base that only partially ionizes.

explain.title: Acids in the stomach
explain.body: The stomach produces hydrochloric acid to digest food. Too much acid can cause stomach acidity. Weak bases such as calcium hydroxide and magnesium hydroxide are used in antacids to neutralize stomach acid.

mistakes: Writing OH⁻ as the ion produced by an Arrhenius acid; acids produce H⁺ or H₃O⁺.
Writing H₃O⁺ as the ion produced by an Arrhenius base; bases produce OH⁻.
Confusing acid strength with concentration: strength concerns ionization, while concentration concerns the amount of acid in solution.
Forgetting the charges on ions when writing ionization equations.
Saying that NaCl forms as solid crystals during neutralization in water; the textbook describes hydrated Na⁺ and Cl⁻ spectator ions in solution.

modules.title: 7.3 Bronsted – Lowry concepts of Acids and Bases

writtenQuestions.text:
Q7.2. In the presence of a drop of an acid, water is known to ionize as follows:

H₂O (l) ⇌ H⁺ (aq) + OH⁻ (aq)

In your opinion, which name will be suitable for water: an acid, a base or both?
modelAnswer: Water can act as an acid by donating a proton (H⁺).
Water can act as a base by accepting a proton (H⁺).
Therefore, water can behave as both an acid and a base.
Water is called an amphoteric compound.

examTips: This section can appear as a short-answer question asking you to define a Brønsted–Lowry acid or base, or to identify them in a reaction.
For reaction questions, follow the H⁺: the donor is the acid and the acceptor is the base. Then identify the conjugate acid and conjugate base if asked.
For comparison questions, earn marks by stating both proton definitions and explaining that Brønsted–Lowry reactions do not require water.
For a question about water, use the term amphoteric and explain that water can donate or accept a proton.

hints: Think about what water can do to be an acid and what it can do to be a base.
Water can donate H⁺ or accept H⁺; what is the term for a substance that can do both?
yourTurn.question:
Q7.2. In the presence of a drop of an acid, water is known to ionize as follows:

H₂O (l) ⇌ H⁺ (aq) + OH⁻ (aq)

In your opinion, which name will be suitable for water: an acid, a base or both?
solution: Water can act as an acid by donating a proton (H⁺).
Water can act as a base by accepting a proton (H⁺).
Therefore, water can behave as both an acid and a base.
Water is called an amphoteric compound.
yourTurn.answer: Both; water is amphoteric because it can behave as an acid and as a base.

steps.why: The reaction shows HCl and H₂O as the reactants and the products formed after proton transfer.
HCl gives H⁺ to water, so it is the proton donor and therefore the acid.
H₂O receives H⁺ from HCl, so it is the proton acceptor and therefore the base.
After HCl donates H⁺, Cl⁻ remains as its conjugate base; after H₂O accepts H⁺, H₃O⁺ is its conjugate acid.
steps.text: H₃O⁺ is the conjugate acid and Cl⁻ is the conjugate base.

example.question: For HCl(g) + H₂O(l) ⇌ H₃O⁺(aq) + Cl⁻, identify the acid, base, conjugate acid and conjugate base.
example.answer: HCl is the acid, H₂O is the base, H₃O⁺ is the conjugate acid and Cl⁻ is the conjugate base.

explain.title: The Brønsted–Lowry idea
explain.body: The section gives these definitions: “An acid is a substance that donates a proton.” and “A base is a substance that accepts a proton.” A proton is H⁺. Look for which substance gives H⁺ and which one receives it.

explain.title: How this differs from Arrhenius
explain.body: The Arrhenius definitions require water as the solvent. Brønsted–Lowry uses proton transfer, so the reaction may take place in the gas phase or in the presence of any solvent. A substance does not need to contain OH⁻ to behave as a Brønsted–Lowry base.

explain.title: Conjugate acid and conjugate base
explain.body: When an acid gives away H⁺, the species left is its conjugate base. When a base receives H⁺, the product is its conjugate acid. In HCl + H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + Cl⁻, H₃O⁺ is the conjugate acid and Cl⁻ is the conjugate base.

explain.title: Water can do either job
explain.body: Water accepts H⁺ from HCl, so it acts as a base in that reaction. Water donates H⁺ to NH₃, so it acts as an acid there. A compound that can behave as both an acid and a base is called amphoteric.

mistakes: Do not label an acid or base just by looking for OH⁻; follow the proton transfer.
Do not call the proton acceptor an acid: accepting H⁺ makes it a base.
Do not assume water must be involved in every Brønsted–Lowry acid–base reaction.
Do not confuse a conjugate acid with a conjugate base: accepting H⁺ forms the conjugate acid, while donating H⁺ forms the conjugate base.
When describing water, include both behaviours and the term amphoteric.

examTips: A short-answer question may ask for the products of an acid reacting with a metal, carbonate, alkali or metal oxide. Learn each product pattern.
For reaction questions, write a balanced equation and include state symbols when they are given in your textbook.
For an observation question, state both what is seen and the product that explains it.
In questions about alkalis and ammonium salts, identify ammonia gas as a product.

hints: An acid reacting with a carbonate forms a salt, water and carbon dioxide.
The salt is made from Ba²⁺ and Cl⁻; balance the chloride ions and hydrogen.
yourTurn.question: Which salt is formed when HCl reacts with BaCO₃?
solution: An acid reacting with a carbonate forms a salt, water and carbon dioxide.
The salt formed from barium and chloride ions is BaCl₂.

explain.title: Acids react with alkalis and metal oxides
explain.body: Both reactions produce a salt and water. For example, an acid neutralizes an alkali, while it also reacts with a metal oxide to form salt and water.

explain.title: Acids react with metals and carbonates
explain.body: Reactive metals such as magnesium and zinc react with acids to form salts and release hydrogen gas. Acids react with metal carbonates and hydrogen carbonates to form salts, water and carbon dioxide.

explain.title: Bases and alkalis
explain.body: The textbook defines alkalis as: “alkalis are those bases which are soluble in water.” NaOH and KOH are examples. Calcium hydroxide is sparingly soluble, while copper(II) hydroxide is insoluble.

explain.title: Alkalis release ammonia
explain.body: An alkali reacts with an ammonium salt to form a salt, water and ammonia gas. Remember that ammonia is different from the hydrogen produced in an acid–metal reaction.

mistakes: Do not confuse the gases: reactive metals with acids produce hydrogen, carbonates with acids produce carbon dioxide, and alkalis with ammonium salts produce ammonia.
Do not forget water when writing the products of an acid–carbonate reaction.
Do not say that all bases are alkalis; an alkali is a base that is soluble in water.
Check the number of atoms on both sides so the equation is balanced.

examTips: This section can be tested with a short question asking for the pH range or how acid rain forms.
For a formation question, name SO₂ and NO₂, explain that they mix with moisture, and include the relevant equations if asked to describe the process.
For an effects question, organize your answer by soil and plants, aquatic life, and buildings or other structures.
Write the equations with correct formulae and balancing as printed in your textbook when the question asks for them.

hints: Think about the effects on land and living things in water.
Name the damage to structures as well as the effects on soil, plants, and aquatic life.
yourTurn.question: State the effects of acid rain on soil, plants, aquatic life, and human-made structures.
solution: Acid rain makes soil more acidic.
It dissolves and washes away nutrients needed by plants, and many plants cannot live or grow in acidic soil.
It can make water bodies too acidic for aquatic animals; many lakes, rivers, ponds, and streams no longer have fish.
Acid rain and dry deposition of acidic particles damage buildings, statues, automobiles, and other structures made of stone and metal.
yourTurn.answer: Acid rain makes soil more acidic and washes away nutrients needed by plants. It can damage vegetation, make water too acidic for aquatic animals, and damage buildings, statues, automobiles, and other stone and metal structures.

explain.title: What acid rain is
explain.body: “When rain water has pH between 4.2 – 4.4, it is called acid rain.” Remember this pH range.

explain.title: How acid rain forms
explain.body: Burning fossil fuels releases SO₂ and NO₂. When these gases mix with moisture in air, they form acid droplets that fall to the ground.

explain.title: Effects on soil and plants
explain.body: Acid rain makes soil more acidic and washes away nutrients plants need. It can damage vegetation, and many plants cannot grow in acidic soil.

explain.title: Effects on water and structures
explain.body: Water bodies can become too acidic for aquatic animals. Acid rain and dry acidic particles can also damage buildings, statues, automobiles, and other stone and metal structures.

mistakes: Giving the wrong pH range; the section states 4.2–4.4.
Saying that acid rain forms without mentioning moisture in the air.
Naming only one effect when the question asks about several areas.
Forgetting that dry deposition of acidic particles also damages structures.

explain.title: Two ways to define acids and bases
explain.body: In the Arrhenius concept, an acid produces H⁺ in water and a base produces OH⁻ in water. In the Brønsted–Lowry concept, an acid donates H⁺ and a base accepts H⁺.

explain.title: Acids react in familiar patterns
explain.body: A metal reacting with an acid commonly forms a salt and hydrogen. An acid reacting with a carbonate forms a salt, carbon dioxide and water. An acid reacting with a base or basic oxide forms a salt and water.

explain.title: Acid strength is not concentration
explain.body: Strength describes the extent to which an acid ionizes in water. Concentration describes how much acid is present in a given volume of solution.

explain.title: Conjugate acid–base pairs differ by H⁺
explain.body: When an acid donates H⁺, the species left is its conjugate base. For example, CH₃COOH donates H⁺ to form CH₃COO⁻.

explain.title: Some oxides and ions can act both ways
explain.body: Non-metallic oxides generally show acidic character by reacting with bases. Water and HCO₃⁻ can take part in proton transfer as either an acid or a base.

mistakes: Do not confuse acid strength with acid concentration; one describes ionization and the other amount per volume.
Do not forget that acid–carbonate reactions produce carbon dioxide as well as salt and water.
Balance equations and write correct ion charges in formulas, such as CaSO₄ and BaCl₂.
A conjugate base is formed after an acid loses H⁺; it is not the species formed after gaining H⁺.
For the lime-water test, distinguish the short-duration milky precipitate from the clearing caused by excess CO₂.
Do not claim that every acidic substance must contain an ionised hydrogen already; explain proton transfer or ion formation in water as appropriate.

notes.title: Acids, bases and alkalis
notes.answer: An alkali is a base that dissolves in water.
notes.explanation: An alkali is a base that dissolves in water. Acids and bases have different properties, and when they react in equal amounts they neutralize each other to form salt and water.
notes.simple: Acids and bases are different kinds of substances. A base that dissolves in water is called an alkali.
examples: Sodium hydroxide dissolves in water, so it is an alkali.
Sodium oxide reacts with water to form sodium hydroxide, a base.
steps: Identify whether the substance is an acid or a base.
If it is a base, check whether it dissolves in water.
A base that dissolves in water is an alkali.
notes.checkAnswer: An alkali is a base that dissolves in water.

notes.title: Arrhenius Acids and Bases
notes.answer: Arrhenius acids produce H⁺ or H₃O⁺ in water; Arrhenius bases produce OH⁻ in water.
notes.explanation: The Arrhenius idea classifies acids and bases by what they produce when they dissociate in water. An acid produces H⁺ or H₃O⁺, while a base produces OH⁻. The amount of ionization also helps us describe an acid or base as strong or weak.
notes.simple: In water, acids give H₃O⁺ and bases give OH⁻. Strong substances ionize more completely; weak substances ionize only partly.
examples: HCl ionizes in water to form H₃O⁺ and Cl⁻.
NaOH ionizes in water to form Na⁺ and OH⁻.
steps: An acid is that substance which dissociates in water to give proton (H⁺) or hydronium ion (H₃O⁺).
A base is that substance which dissociates in water to give hydroxyl ions (OH⁻).
For example: HCl(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ H₃O⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq).
For example: NaOH(aq) → Na⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq).
Acid strength depends upon the extent to which it is ionized in water.
notes.checkQuestion: Why is NaOH an Arrhenius base?
notes.checkAnswer: NaOH is an Arrhenius base because it dissociates in water to give OH⁻ ions.

notes.title: Brønsted–Lowry Acids and Bases
notes.answer: An acid donates a proton; a base accepts a proton.
notes.explanation: In the Brønsted–Lowry concept, an acid gives a proton and a base takes a proton. Water can do either, depending on what it reacts with.
notes.simple: An acid hands over H⁺. A base receives H⁺. Water can do either job.
examples: HCl gives a proton to H₂O, so HCl is the acid and H₂O is the base.
NH₃ takes a proton from H₂O, so NH₃ is the base and H₂O is the acid.
steps: Find which substance donates H⁺: it is the acid.
Find which substance accepts H⁺: it is the base.
The acid left after donating H⁺ is its conjugate base.
The base formed after accepting H⁺ is its conjugate acid.
notes.checkQuestion: What is a substance called if it can behave as both an acid and a base?
notes.checkAnswer: Water is amphoteric because it can behave as both an acid and a base.

notes.title: Reactions of Acids and Bases
notes.answer: Acids react with metals, alkalis or metal oxides, and carbonates in characteristic ways. Alkalis also release ammonia from ammonium salts.
notes.explanation: Acids react with alkalis or metal oxides to make salt and water, with reactive metals to make salt and hydrogen, and with carbonates to make salt, water and carbon dioxide. Alkalis also react with ammonium salts to release ammonia.
notes.simple: Different substances react with acids and bases in different ways, often making a salt and a gas.
steps: Identify the type of substance reacting with the acid.
Use the matching products: metal gives salt and hydrogen; carbonate gives salt, water and carbon dioxide.
Write and balance the chemical equation.
notes.checkQuestion: What products form when an acid reacts with a metal carbonate?
notes.checkAnswer: Salt, water and carbon dioxide are formed.

notes.title: Acid Rain and its Effects
notes.answer: Acid rain is rain water with a pH between 4.2 and 4.4.
notes.explanation: Acid rain forms when harmful gases from burning fossil fuels mix with moisture in the air. It can harm soil, plants, aquatic life, and structures.
notes.simple: Some gases mix with water in the air and fall as acidic rain. This can hurt living things and damage buildings.
examples: SO₂ forms SO₃, which then reacts with water to form H₂SO₄.
Acid rain can make lakes too acidic for fish to live in.
steps: Burning fossil fuels releases harmful gases, including SO₂ and NO₂.
The gases mix with moisture in the air and form acid droplets.
The droplets fall to the ground as acid rain.
Acid rain harms soil, plants, aquatic life, and structures.
notes.checkQuestion: Name two effects of acid rain.
notes.checkAnswer: Acid rain can harm soil and plants, make water too acidic for aquatic animals, and damage buildings and other structures.

notes.title: Acids and Bases: Key Ideas
notes.answer: An acid donates H⁺; a base accepts H⁺. Acid–base reactions form products such as salts, water, carbon dioxide or hydrogen, depending on the reactants.
notes.explanation: Acids and bases can be described by the ions they produce in water or by proton transfer. Acids react with some metals, carbonates and bases in characteristic ways. Some substances, such as water and hydrogen carbonate ions, can act as either acids or bases.
notes.simple: An acid can give away a proton, H⁺. A base can accept H⁺. In water, acids produce H₃O⁺ and bases produce OH⁻ or accept H⁺. Reactions help us identify acids and bases.
steps: Identify the acid and base using the definition named in the question.
For a reaction, write the correct products and balance the equation.
For proton transfer, show which species loses H⁺ and which gains H⁺.
For an acid–carbonate reaction, include salt, water and carbon dioxide.
notes.checkQuestion: How does HSO₄⁻ show that it is a Brønsted–Lowry acid?
notes.checkAnswer: HSO₄⁻ donates H⁺ to form SO₄²⁻, so it acts as a Brønsted–Lowry acid.
